title: Logical connections
summary: Choose linking words that show contrast, cause, condition, addition and sequence, and that keep the meaning clear across sentences.

sections.title: What is the link?
content: Read these two ideas: ‘The shop was closed. We walked home.’ They could be joined in more than one way, but the meaning changes.
‘The shop was closed, so we walked home’ gives a result. ‘The shop was closed, but we stayed nearby’ gives a surprise. Before you choose a linking word, ask what the second idea does to the first.

sections.title: Five common links
content: Contrast shows a surprise or a difference: but, although, however. Cause and result show why or what happened next: because, so, therefore.
Condition shows what must be true: if, unless. Addition gives another point: and, also, in addition. Sequence shows order: then, after that, finally.
Check the grammar too. Although and because join two clauses in one sentence. However and therefore usually start a new sentence and take a comma.

sections.title: Test the meaning, then the grammar
content: Consider: ‘The film was long. ___, nobody left the hall.’ Being long might make people leave, but nobody did. That is a surprise, so the link is contrast. However fits, and because it starts a new sentence, it takes a comma.

Now consider: ‘The ferry was late ___ the sea was rough.’ The rough sea explains the delay, so the link is cause. Because fits. So would reverse the logic, because it would make the delay cause the rough sea.
A relative word links an extra detail to a noun. Use who for people and which for things: ‘The guide who met us spoke three languages.’

sections.title: Name the link first
content: For these two items, say the link in your own words before you look at the options: surprise, reason, condition, extra point or order. Then choose the word that shows it.

sections.title: Choose without the label
content: Now choose the linking word without naming the link first. Read the whole sentence, or both sentences, and then read it again with your choice in place.
If two options look possible, ask which one keeps the meaning of the full text.

sections.title: Find where it went wrong
content: Meaning error: I chose a word showing the wrong link, such as a result where the text shows a surprise. Grammar error: the link was right, but the word does not fit the sentence, such as however joining two clauses after a comma.
Direction error: I chose the right kind of link but reversed cause and result. Reading error: I looked only at the words next to the gap.

sections.title: Try a new text
content: Complete one unseen short text with two linked gaps. If you need a hint or get it wrong, you will try a new text with different events, so you practise the skill and not the answer.
